Text as Data: Words, Weights and Context

A Course on Data Visualization

Livio Finos, University of Padova

1 The question we will investigate

Main question: How do our choices about representing text change what we see?

Units 11 and 12 compared objects through distances. We now need to decide what the measurements of a text document should be. Before making a map, we will read texts, count words, choose weights, and check how much context is lost.

Use these notes during class and keep them for review. Every worked BBC example is followed by a task on a different corpus: SMS messages. This transfer is deliberate: short informal messages need not behave like news articles.

A token is one occurrence of a small piece of text produced by a splitting rule. In this unit, think of it informally as a word occurrence: tea tea cake contains three tokens, even though it has only two different word forms. Tokenisation means splitting text into these units. We will examine the precise splitting and filtering rules later; this first definition lets us describe document length before studying those choices.

1.1 Learning goals

  • Define a document, a token, metadata and a document-term matrix (DTM).
  • Explain how tokenisation and vocabulary filtering alter the data.
  • Distinguish counts, relative frequencies and TF-IDF weights.
  • Compare word clouds with ordered bars and interpret n-grams in context.
  • Read directed bigram networks and use their paths to propose longer phrases that can be checked in the original texts.
  • Keep a reproducible record of decisions and their consequences.

1.2 What you need

Prerequisites: R indexing, tables, proportions, simple plots and matrices. R packages: ggplot2, knitr and rmarkdown. The inspectable helpers in data/text_helpers.R use base R; no specialist text-mining package is required.

Open the course folder (the folder containing these Rmd files and data/). Keep a script called 13_my_text_lab.R. Append an answer after each activity; do not overwrite earlier results when changing a setting. A useful entry is prediction -> code -> output -> interpretation -> limitation.

2 Data and context

The guided corpus contains 250 real BBC articles, 50 in each of five topics. Your activity corpus contains 240 real SMS messages, 120 labelled ham (ordinary messages) and 120 spam. Exact text duplicates were removed before sampling. The full downloaded archives contained 2,225 BBC articles and 5,574 SMS rows; after exact-text deduplication, 2,127 and 5,171 unique texts remained.

One complete article or message is one document. Sentences are temporary units for extracting adjacent words; they will not become separate MDS points.

Column Meaning Analytical role
document_id Unique retained document Row label
text Original complete text Source of features
category BBC topic or SMS label Metadata; excluded from word features
source_id Original file path or row Traceability
raw_tokens Baseline token count, calculated by the import helper Derived document-length measure; not an original CSV column

The files retain the original text. English ASCII-letter tokenisation below is a simple baseline, not a language-independent linguistic parser. These older corpora do not represent all present-day news or messaging.

library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
source("data/text_helpers.R")
bbc <- load_text_docs("data/bbc_articles_250.csv")
sms <- load_text_docs("data/sms_messages_240.csv")

3 Begin with documents, not with a cloud

Read a few articles before calculating summaries. Check identifiers, category counts and length. The import helper creates raw_tokens: the number of baseline word tokens in each complete document, counting repeated occurrences. For this initial count it lowercases text, recognises English-letter sequences with internal apostrophes, drops single-letter words and excludes numeric tokens. It has not yet removed stopwords or applied a document-frequency filter.

Thus raw_tokens is a document-length measure, not a list of tokens or a count of distinct words. It follows the stated rule rather than a universal definition of a word. We will inspect and change that rule in the next section.

table(bbc$category)
#> 
#>      business entertainment      politics         sport          tech 
#>            50            50            50            50            50
summary(bbc$raw_tokens)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>   108.0   241.0   350.0   383.8   477.8  2257.0
head(bbc[c("document_id", "category", "raw_tokens")])
# Read the full first article in the R console when discussing its context:
# cat(bbc$text[1])
ggplot(bbc, aes(category, raw_tokens)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.12, seed = 13),
             alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "BBC topic", y = "Baseline tokens per article")

Each point is an article, not a word. Boxplots summarise article-length distributions.

Reading the figure. The vertical scale is document length. Different topics can have different typical lengths, and documents in the same topic also vary. A larger total word count in a group could reflect longer texts, more texts, or both. Labels are useful for checking our map later, not for defining distance.

Your dataset: SMS. Question: Are the SMS messages comparable in length and how does their unit differ from a news article?

Before running R, write a prediction and discuss it with a partner. Then:

  1. Verify identifiers, missing text and category counts. Read two messages per label.
  2. Report median and range of baseline token counts by label and make a length plot.
  3. Explain why a balanced sample cannot estimate the prevalence of spam.
table(sms$category)
summary(sms$raw_tokens)
# Add the within-label summaries, plot and four contextual readings.

Record and compare: save the requested output, explain what it shows in two or three sentences, and compare your prediction with a neighbouring group. Agree on one limitation. Rotate who writes the code and who checks the result.

4 Decide what becomes a token

Our word_tokens() function lowercases text, recognises letter sequences with internal apostrophes, and discards single-letter words. Its optional numeric-token rule retains digit sequences. Punctuation, emojis, URLs and hyphens are not interpreted semantically; URL pieces can survive as words. Inspect the function before treating its output as a complete description.

A stopword list removes selected common words. It is a modelling choice, not an objective definition of useless language. Our short supplied list keeps no, not and never. Check contractions and domain-specific expressions before interpreting meaning or sentiment.

bbc_tokens <- word_tokens(bbc$text)
bbc_clean <- word_tokens(bbc$text, stop_words = course_stopwords)
raw_counts <- term_counts(bbc_tokens)
clean_counts <- term_counts(bbc_clean)
head(raw_counts, 10)
head(clean_counts, 10)
top_bars(setNames(clean_counts$count, clean_counts$term),
         "BBC: frequent retained words", ylab = "Token occurrences")

Corpus-level counts: a long article contributes more tokens than a short article.

Interpretation. Removal changes both the vocabulary and the denominator of later proportions. A term can become relatively frequent without gaining any occurrences. Names, abbreviations and spelling variants remain separate forms.

Stemming reduces related forms to a common stem (possibly not a word). Lemmatisation aims at dictionary forms using linguistic information. Neither is applied in the core analysis. For example, combining run and running changes a column definition; a guessed suffix rule is not reliable lemmatisation.

Before running R, write a prediction and discuss it with a partner. Then:

  4. Use grep() on token names to find related word forms; propose one merge and one reason it might be inappropriate. Do not implement guessed lemmatisation.
sms_words <- word_tokens(sms$text)
sms_clean <- word_tokens(sms$text, stop_words = course_stopwords)
# Compare term_counts(), numeric tokens, and an original message.

5 From words to a common document-term matrix

Let CitC_{it} count term tt in document ii. Every row uses the same vocabulary. Rows are documents and columns are terms; metadata never enter this matrix. A zero means no retained occurrence, not missing information. Word order has been discarded: this is a bag-of-words representation.

toy <- c("tea tea cake", "tea bread", "bread cake")
toy_C <- make_dtm(word_tokens(toy), c("D1", "D2", "D3"), min_df = 1)
toy_C
#>    bread cake tea
#> D1     0    1   2
#> D2     1    0   1
#> D3     1    1   0
bbc_C <- make_dtm(bbc_clean, bbc$document_id, min_df = 2)
c(documents = nrow(bbc_C), terms = ncol(bbc_C),
  zero_fraction = mean(bbc_C == 0), empty_rows = sum(rowSums(bbc_C) == 0))
#>     documents         terms zero_fraction    empty_rows 
#>   250.0000000  5027.0000000     0.9721241     0.0000000

Document frequency dft=∑iI(Cit>0)df_t=\sum_i I(C_{it}>0) counts documents containing a term, not its total occurrences. The threshold min_df=2 retains terms found in at least two documents. This reduces isolated spellings and singleton terms, but may discard meaningful rare words. It is not a statistical significance rule.

chosen_terms <- head(names(sort(colSums(bbc_C), decreasing = TRUE)), 10)
small <- bbc_C[seq(1, 250, length.out = 10), chosen_terms]
heatmap(small, Rowv = NA, Colv = NA, scale = "none",
        margins = c(7, 8), col = hcl.colors(20, "Blues 3"))

Counts for ten selected articles and ten frequent terms. Rows and columns are not clustered or standardised.

sms_clean <- word_tokens(sms$text, stop_words = course_stopwords)
C_sms_all <- make_dtm(sms_clean, sms$document_id, min_df = 2)

6 Frequent and distinctive are different questions

Work with one corpus at a time, after choosing its stopwords and retained vocabulary and excluding documents that have no retained terms. Before using the formula, define its ingredients:

  • NN is the number of retained documents in that corpus. The document index is i=1,…,Ni=1,\ldots,N; here one document is one complete article or SMS.
  • VV is the number of distinct retained terms in the common vocabulary. A term is a word form used as a matrix column. The index t=1,…,Vt=1,\ldots,V identifies the term of interest; ss is another index that runs through the same vocabulary when we sum over terms.
  • CitC_{it} is the number of occurrences of term tt in document ii. This is a cell of the document-term count matrix CC; repetitions count.
  • Li=∑s=1VCisL_i=\sum_{s=1}^{V}C_{is} is the total number of retained token occurrences in document ii. It is positive for every retained document. It generally differs from raw_tokens, which was calculated before stopword removal and vocabulary filtering.
  • I(Cit>0)I(C_{it}>0) is an indicator: it equals 1 if document ii contains at least one occurrence of term tt, and 0 otherwise.

We can now define four related quantities:

pit=CitLi,dft=∑i=1NI(Cit>0),p_{it}=\frac{C_{it}}{L_i},\qquad df_t=\sum_{i=1}^{N}I(C_{it}>0),

idft=log⁡(Ndft),Wit=pitidft.idf_t=\log\left(\frac{N}{df_t}\right),\qquad W_{it}=p_{it}\,idf_t.

  1. Term frequency (TF), pitp_{it}: the proportion of retained tokens in document ii that are term tt. The proportions sum to one within each document. Here TF means a proportion, not a raw count.
  2. Document frequency, dftdf_t: the number of retained documents containing term tt. Each document contributes at most one, however often it repeats the term. For a retained term, 1≤dft≤N1\leq df_t\leq N.
  3. Inverse document frequency (IDF), idftidf_t: the natural logarithm of N/dftN/df_t. It is a corpus-level weight, shared by all documents for that term. A term appearing in fewer documents receives a larger IDF; a term appearing in every document has idft=log⁡(1)=0idf_t=\log(1)=0.
  4. TF-IDF, WitW_{it}: the product of the within-document proportion and the corpus-level IDF. The matrix WW has the same document rows and term columns as CC, but its entries are weights rather than counts. A large value identifies a term that is relatively frequent in this document and not widespread across the corpus; it does not establish universal importance.

A constructed numerical example. Suppose a term occurs 4 times among 100 retained tokens in one document and occurs in 10 of the corpus’s 50 retained documents. Its TF is 4/100=0.044/100=0.04, its document frequency is 10, its IDF is log⁡(50/10)=log⁡(5)\log(50/10)=\log(5), and its TF-IDF in that document is 0.04log⁡(5)≈0.06440.04\log(5)\approx 0.0644. The four occurrences count four times for TF, but this document contributes only one to document frequency. These numbers illustrate the formula; they are not a measured BBC result.

We use the natural logarithm and no additive smoothing. Software defaults differ, so report this convention and the retained-token denominator. The same count can get different weights in different corpora. If every term appears in every document, all IDFs are zero; a zero TF-IDF vector cannot be normalised for cosine comparisons.

Before normalising, remove and report empty rows once. Use that common document set for all representations. prepare_text() performs this check and stops on zero TF-IDF norms rather than inventing values.

demo <- prepare_text(bbc)
lab <- prepare_text(sms)
demo$removed
#> character(0)
lab$removed
#>  [1] "sms_0887" "sms_2350" "sms_2964" "sms_3399" "sms_3935" "sms_3997"
#>  [7] "sms_4366" "sms_4825" "sms_4938" "sms_5322"
R_bbc <- demo$representation
R_sms <- lab$representation
stopifnot(all(abs(rowSums(R_bbc$P) - 1) < 1e-12))
selected_id <- rownames(R_bbc$C)[1]
profile <- data.frame(term = colnames(R_bbc$C),
                      count = R_bbc$C[selected_id, ],
                      tf = R_bbc$P[selected_id, ], idf = R_bbc$idf,
                      tfidf = R_bbc$W[selected_id, ])
head(profile[order(-profile$tfidf), ], 10)
top_bars(setNames(profile$tfidf, profile$term),
         "One BBC article: distinctive terms", ylab = "TF-IDF")

Article-level TF-IDF: a high bar means distinctive within this retained BBC corpus, not universally important.

7 A word cloud needs a named quantity

For a topic-level summary, we will average article-level TF-IDF values, including zeros for articles without the term. This gives articles equal weight. It differs from pooling tokens, where long articles contribute more.

business <- demo$docs$category == "business"
topic_weights <- colMeans(R_bbc$W[business, , drop = FALSE])
shown <- head(sort(topic_weights, decreasing = TRUE), 20)
top_bars(shown, "Business: mean article TF-IDF", n = 20,
         ylab = "Mean TF-IDF, including zeros")

Bars and cloud use the same twenty terms and weights. Cloud position is a layout choice, not a semantic coordinate. 

draw_cloud(shown, n = 20, seed = 13)

Bars and cloud use the same twenty terms and weights. Cloud position is a layout choice, not a semantic coordinate.

Reading the figures. Bars have a common baseline and support direct comparisons. In the cloud, font size encodes weight, but rendered area also depends on word length. Position, proximity and direction have no analytic meaning. The supplied packing helper uses font size proportional to an affine function of square-root weight; it does not promise area-proportional encoding. A cloud is an overview, not a substitute for numerical comparison.

is_spam <- lab$docs$category == "spam"

8 Recover a little order with n-grams

A bigram is a pair of adjacent tokens; a trigram has three. Extract them before deleting words, and avoid crossing sentence or document boundaries. Only afterwards filter n-grams containing stopwords. Otherwise removing of from the constructed phrase bank of england would invent bank england. The phrase is a teaching illustration, not an extracted BBC quotation.

phrase <- "bank of england"
sentence_ngrams(phrase, filter_stop = FALSE)
#> [1] "bank of"    "of england"
word_tokens(phrase, stop_words = course_stopwords)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "bank"    "england"
bbc_bigrams <- lapply(bbc$text, sentence_ngrams)
bigram_counts <- term_counts(bbc_bigrams)
top_bars(setNames(bigram_counts$count, bigram_counts$term),
         "BBC: retained adjacent bigrams", ylab = "Bigram occurrences")

Bigrams are adjacent retained word sequences from within approximate sentence boundaries.

Our sentence splitter is punctuation-based; abbreviations and unusual SMS punctuation can defeat it. The baseline word rule also ignores punctuation inside a sentence. Read contextual examples before treating any pair as a linguistically validated expression. Same-document co-occurrence is a different relationship from adjacency and can connect words many sentences apart.

8.1 From bigram counts to a directed word network

The bigram table also defines a directed network:

  • A node is a distinct word form, not an individual token occurrence.
  • An arrow from word aa to word bb means that bb follows aa in at least one extracted bigram. The reverse order would be a different arrow.
  • The edge weight is the number of occurrences of that ordered pair across the corpus. Thicker arrows represent more occurrences. A separate documents column counts how many different texts contain the pair.

The network retains the within-sentence extraction and stopword rules above. It is an adjacency network, not a same-document co-occurrence network and not a diagram of causal effects.

bbc_edges <- bigram_edges(bbc_bigrams, min_count = 10, top_n = 40)
head(bbc_edges)
bbc_network <- plot_bigram_network(bbc_edges, max_components = 3,
                                   title = "BBC: which words follow which?")
bbc_network$plot

BBC directed bigram network. Arrow width encodes occurrences. Shown: the three largest components with at least three words, after retaining at most forty non-self bigrams occurring at least ten times. Panels separate disconnected parts of this filtered graph.

Reading the network. Follow the arrowheads to read order. Several outgoing arrows from mr show alternative continuations of a reporting convention; this hub need not represent the most important topic. Other components suggest names, multiword expressions or source-attribution patterns. These are starting points for reading the articles, not automatically discovered topics.

To keep labels readable, the display selects frequent edges, omits repeated-word self-loops, and shows only the three largest components of at least three nodes. A component is a set connected when arrow direction is ignored. The original bigram table is unchanged. A missing edge or disconnected panel can be a consequence of the display filter; it does not prove absence from the full corpus. The layout separates labels: geometric distance and edge crossings have no semantic meaning. All plotting code is in the supplied helper file; no extra R package is required.

8.2 Let paths suggest longer n-grams, then verify them

A directed path a→b→ca\to b\to c suggests the candidate trigram a b c. But its two edges may come from different sentences or different documents: their presence does not establish that all three words occurred together. Even if both edges are frequent, the longer phrase can be absent. Extract trigrams from the original texts to answer that question.

candidates <- candidate_trigrams(bbc_network$edges)
path_check <- verify_phrases(candidates, bbc$text, n = 3)
knitr::kable(path_check, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Candidate three-word paths and their actual within-sentence trigram counts.")
Candidate three-word paths and their actual within-sentence trigram counts.
phrase actual_occurrences
told bbc news 4
jamie foxx actress 14
actor jamie foxx 14
said mr blair 3
said mr ebbers 0
said mr sullivan 1
said mr howard 0
said mr brown 1
said mr blunkett 4
bbc news website 15

Interpretation. The table contains both observed phrases and candidates with count zero. The graph is therefore useful for proposing expressions; the ordered source tokens decide whether those expressions really occur. Compare the two-edge paths with the longer name/reporting sequences visible in the other components. A path with three arrows suggests four words:

verify_phrases("actor jamie foxx actress", bbc$text, n = 4)

This four-gram is checked as an actual sequence, rather than inferred by multiplying edge weights or taking their minimum. Bigram weights alone do not determine trigram or four-gram frequencies. Longer n-grams retain more context but usually have less support. Compare the count of an expression with the number of source documents containing it before calling it a general pattern. Changing an edge threshold can also break a visible path without changing any original text.

Your dataset: SMS. Question: Which longer expressions does a bigram network suggest, and which actually occur?

Before running R, write a prediction and discuss it with a partner. Then:

  6. Replot with min_count=4, keeping top_n=40. Describe which visible connections change. Retain the extraction order: do not delete stopwords before identifying adjacent sequences.
sms_bigrams <- lapply(sms$text, sentence_ngrams)
sms_edges <- bigram_edges(sms_bigrams, min_count = 2, top_n = 40)
# Draw the network, propose paths, check n-grams and inspect source messages.

9 Sensitivity: a threshold changes what can be represented

The document-frequency threshold is part of the feature definition. Compare BBC thresholds before choosing the more attractive plot.

bbc_df5 <- make_dtm(bbc_clean, bbc$document_id, min_df = 5)
data.frame(min_df = c(2,5),
           vocabulary = c(ncol(bbc_C), ncol(bbc_df5)),
           empty = c(sum(rowSums(bbc_C)==0), sum(rowSums(bbc_df5)==0)))

10 Bring the choices together

Before moving to distances, keep the document IDs, feature definitions and weights together. A visually distinctive word may be a name, a formatting artifact or a rare spelling; an appealing cloud does not validate the pipeline.

11 Check your understanding

Q1. A term occurs ten times in one document and once in each of ten other documents. What are its total count and document frequency?

Q2. Why can a word have a positive count but zero TF-IDF?

Q3. Does proximity in a word cloud imply semantic similarity?

Q4. Why retain complete messages as rows even when extracting sentence-level n-grams?

Q5. If both a b and b c occur in the corpus, must a b c occur? How would you check rather than infer it from the network?

12 Take-home messages

  • A corpus is a collection of defined observational units, not just a bag of files.
  • Preprocessing changes the variables; record the choices and inspect original texts.
  • Counts, proportions and TF-IDF answer different questions.
  • A word cloud needs explicit weights and does not supply a semantic geometry.
  • Adjacent n-grams must be extracted before word deletion; verify their context.
  • Directed bigram paths suggest longer phrases but cannot establish their presence or frequency. Check the original ordered tokens.
  • Empty profiles must be handled explicitly before comparing documents.
